parsed.explanation: The division is among the fifteen most protective jurisdictions: gender-identity public-accommodation law since 2008, hate-crime enhancement, trans-panic defence repeal, X markers on licences and birth certificates, a 2023 care shield law, and no mapped facility ban. But the combined regime includes the national layer, which the dossier states applies here: sex-binary entry screening with fraud/lifetime-ineligibility referral on document discrepancy, foreign-government travel advisories, a federal single-sex facility exclusion, conversion-therapy-style federal prison policy, documented immigration-detention abuse, and official threat framing. State protections do not pre-empt these; litigation is unresolved, so no remedy is shown working. Outed consequences are moderate-to-severe at borders, federal facilities and custody, mild-to-protected elsewhere.

entry_documents.exposure: National Feb 2025 cable instructs refusal where documents or records cast reasonable doubt on sex, plus fraud analysis supporting possible lifetime ineligibility; passport X markers barred; foreign governments issued travel advisories and reported confiscations/strandings abroad. Documented.
entry_documents.protection: Division recognises X markers on licences/birth certificates and bars gender-identity discrimination in public services;入境 screening remains federal. Existing foreign X passports valid until expiry. Partial, subordinate.
entry_documents.interaction: State document accessibility cannot cure a federal entry refusal; a document discrepancy can escalate from screening to fraud finding and detention, moving the traveller into the custody exposure. Status: documented.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style inmate policies (haircut, hormone removal, substituted psychiatric drugs) from 2026; immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary and severe sexual abuse of trans men. Division hate-crime law does not reach federal custody.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division hate-crime penalties, 2021 trans-panic-defence ban, and equality law; no division-specific custody data exists. Enforcement against custody abuse not documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor detained federally (entry dispute, visa issue) enters the federal regime regardless of division protections; the dossier documents no pre-emption or shield here. Status: documented federally, division practice not_documented.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities; equality map shows widening state bans elsewhere, four states with criminal triggers. These reach federal buildings, airports and national sites a visitor enters within the division.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no mapped facility ban, sits in the 'Most Protective' tier, and its 2008 equality law covers public accommodation and public services uniformly statewide.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Two regimes coexist: division facilities are open, federal facilities within them are not; no documented conflict rule or exemption for visitors. Status: documented at both levels.

care_services.exposure: National Oct 2025 proposed rules and funding actions target trans care; DOJ subpoenaed under-19 patient records in 2025. Shield-law scope after 2023 amendments is unresolved in sources.
care_services.protection: Division shield law (2023) protects patients/providers from out-of-jurisdiction charges; public insurance covers gender-affirming care; equality law covers public services.
care_services.interaction: Shield protects a care-seeking visitor from division prosecution, but cannot bind federal investigators or federal funding conditions. Status: documented state protection, federal interaction partially documented.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' groups; DOJ reward memo uses 'radical gender ideology' language; official framing of care as 'mutilation'. Elevated discovery and hostility risk nationally.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division repealed the mental-health law equating trans people with paedophilia (2019), funds no comparable rhetoric, and sits in the top protective tier; national memo does not list trans status as a reward criterion.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal framing raises the stakes of any federal encounter (screening, federal building) while the division's own institutions remain non-hostile. Status: documented.

minors_guardians.exposure: National orders direct criminal investigation/prosecution of teachers facilitating a minor's social transition and target youth care; a parent travelling with a trans minor could face scrutiny if records cast doubt on sex or purpose of travel.
minors_guardians.protection: Division bans conversion therapy on minors since 2015, maintains trans-inclusive schools policy upheld through 2020, and its shield law covers care legal in-division for minors arriving from banning jurisdictions.
minors_guardians.interaction: Division shield protects the care visit itself; federal entry screening and record-subpoena exposure are not displaced. Status: documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific data on police stops, searches or violence against trans visitors; national bias statistics show persistent anti-LGB bias incidents. Absence of data is not safety.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division hate-crime statute adds penalties for gender-identity bias; equality law covers public accommodations; gay/trans panic defences abolished 2021; only 23 states cover gender identity in bias statutes nationally.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State charging/prosecution statistics for gender-identity hate crimes were not found, so operative enforcement is uncertain. Status: uncertain.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: National passport suit, executive-order challenges and health rules remain unresolved; enforcement of the division public-accommodations law against venues excluding trans patrons is undocumented; nationwide equality maps note other laws may still restrict access.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active civil-liberties litigation, a legal-aid passport FAQ, division equality law in force since 2008, shield law, and a top-tier protective ranking.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Paper state protections operate, but federal measures are contested without injunctions in force in several areas; practical exposure varies by moment of travel. Status: documented with material unknowns.

anchor_checks.comparison: Higher than 0.35-A: there the birth-sex facility rule covers all public buildings, is court-upheld with rejected complaints and no foreigner exemption. Here the division imposes no facility ban, provides accommodation law, hate-crime penalties and a care shield; only the narrower federal facility and entry regimes are unremedied, so the tier-one exposure is thinner in scope and partially counterweighted.

Mixed against 0.55-B: its parent has no facility restriction, while this federal layer has documented universal entry screening, a facility exclusion and severe custody practice — harsher at the border/federal stages. But the division's documented protections (accommodation enforcement statutes, shield law, X markers, hate-crime penalties) exceed that province's mediators. Net: roughly comparable, slightly below on federal exposure, above on state protection.

Lower than 0.75-C: there the only legal residue is a dead-letter statute with documented acceptance, working courts and identity-based facility access. Here federal exposure is live and current — refusal/ fraud referral at entry, facility exclusion, custody conversion-therapy policy, official threat framing — with challenges unresolved, not dead-letter.

Similar to 0.45-D: a documented universal federal exposure (invasive screening/facility exclusion) acknowledged by oversight yet persisting without effective remedy, set against generally accepting society and convicted attackers elsewhere. The division's stronger, in-force equality and shield statutes place it at the top of that comparison, hence mid-point scoring.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two regimes at once. Within the division, law is among the country's most protective: gender-identity public accommodation since 2008, hate-crime enhancement, trans-panic repeal, X markers, and a 2023 shield law — all in force, though enforcement statistics are missing. At the border, in federal buildings, and in federal custody, the national regime operates unaltered: document discrepancy can trigger refusal and fraud referral, government-funded single-sex facilities exclude by birth sex, and detained trans people face conversion-therapy-style policy or documented abuse — with litigation pending rather than relief granted. State protections cushion street, service and care encounters; they do not pre-empt federal stages, and no operative pre-emption or refusal is documented. The result is moderate overall risk: safe and protected in most of the itinerary, materially exposed at entry, federal facilities and any detention.
